macro-aims-explorer:
Analyse 6 marks Analyse how pursuing economic growth could clash with keeping the balance of payments stable. (Oct/Nov 2024, P22)
ReminderBuild a chain from growth to incomes, imports and exports.

Economic growth may raise employment and incomes. People could then buy more imports. Firms may also switch output to the busier home market, so exports fall and a current account deficit could appear or widen.

Producing more may need imported raw materials and capital goods. If growth also causes inflation, domestic products may become less price competitive, reducing exports further.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse the ways in which lowering interest rates could cause one macroeconomic aim to clash with another. (Oct/Nov 2022, P21)
ReminderName two aims in each conflict and show the chain from the interest rate.

A lower interest rate is likely to reduce saving and encourage borrowing and spending. Higher total demand may raise output and employment, but could also cause demand-pull inflation, so full employment and stable prices may conflict.

Higher spending may include more imports. The current account deficit could widen, so economic growth may conflict with balance of payments stability. Borrowers and owners of firms may gain while savers receive less, which could conflict with a fairer distribution of income.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not better education can help a government to meet its macroeconomic aims. (Oct/Nov 2024, P21)
ReminderLink education to at least two aims on each side, then judge. Costs, time lags and emigration weaken the case.

Better education may raise workers’ skills and productivity. Output could grow, and the economy’s productive capacity may increase, supporting economic growth. Better qualified workers are likely to find jobs more easily, so unemployment may fall. Higher productivity could lower average costs, which may ease inflation and make exports more competitive, improving the current account.

Education spending has an opportunity cost. Extra government spending may raise total demand and cause inflation, or require higher taxes. The benefits could take many years to appear, and some skilled workers may emigrate. Courses may teach skills that employers do not want.

Overall, education is likely to help most aims in the long run, but only if it matches the skills firms need and enough jobs exist. In the short run other policies may be needed.
ig-fiscal-budget:
Define 2 marks Define government budget. (May/June 2023, P23)
ReminderA plan, covering both spending and revenue.

A government budget is a plan, or forecast, of government spending and government revenue for a period.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse what could cause a government to collect more tax revenue. (May/June 2023, P21)
ReminderLink each cause to a particular tax.

Tax revenue is the money a government raises from taxes. Higher employment is likely to raise incomes, so income tax receipts may rise. More consumer spending could increase indirect tax revenue. Higher profits may raise corporation tax revenue.

A government may raise tax rates or widen the tax base to cover more goods or people. Better collection and less evasion, for example through simpler forms or less corruption, could also increase revenue.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not supply-side policies will shrink a government’s budget deficit. (Feb/March 2025, P22)
ReminderA budget deficit is spending above revenue. Do not confuse it with a current account deficit.

Supply-side policies aim to raise productive capacity. Education and training may raise productivity, growth and employment, bringing in more income and spending taxes while benefit spending falls. Privatisation could bring in sales revenue and remove support for loss-making state firms.

However, training, subsidies and tax cuts cost money or reduce revenue, so the deficit may widen in the short run. The policies may take years to work, or may fail if there is little demand for the extra output.

The deficit is likely to fall only if the extra revenue in the long run outweighs the early cost. Cheaper measures such as privatisation or deregulation may help sooner than education.
ig-fiscal-spending:
Analyse 6 marks Analyse ways in which more government spending could make an economy grow faster. (Feb/March 2021, P22)
ReminderShow both the demand effect and the effect on productive capacity.

Government spending is part of total demand, so a rise may increase output. Firms could respond by employing more workers and investing.

Spending on education, health care or infrastructure may raise productivity and lower costs. This could increase productive capacity and attract foreign firms. Subsidies may encourage firms to produce more, and benefits may raise the spending of poorer households.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not an economy gains when its government spends more on housing. (May/June 2024, P22)
ReminderWeigh jobs and living standards against opportunity cost.

More housing spending is likely to raise total demand. Output and employment in construction may rise, house prices or rents could fall, and homelessness and poverty may be reduced, raising living standards.

The money has an opportunity cost. Taxes or borrowing may have to rise, building could create external costs, and extra demand may cause inflation. Private firms might provide better housing.

The economy is more likely to gain where there is a housing shortage and unemployed resources. If the economy is near full capacity or the homes are poor quality, the money could do more elsewhere.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not heavy government spending can help to achieve the government’s macroeconomic aims. (Oct/Nov 2021, P21)
ReminderCover at least two aims on each side.

High spending raises total demand. This may bring economic growth and lower unemployment, especially through public projects. Spending on education could raise skills, subsidies to exporters may help the current account, and welfare spending could redistribute income.

However, higher total demand may cause demand-pull inflation. More incomes could increase imports, and generous benefits might reduce the incentive to work. The spending may require higher taxes or borrowing.

It is likely to help when there is spare capacity and the money raises productivity. Near full employment it could mainly add to inflation, so the type of spending matters.
ig-fiscal-taxation:
Identify 2 marks Identify two features that a good tax should have. (Feb/March 2021, P22)
ReminderEquity, certainty, convenience, economy, efficiency, flexibility.

It should be fair, based on people’s ability to pay. It should be cheap to collect compared with the revenue raised.

Explain 4 marks Explain how a progressive tax differs from a regressive one. (Feb/March 2020, P22)
ReminderCompare the proportion of income taken, not the amount paid.

A progressive tax takes a larger proportion of income as income rises, so it is likely to make incomes more evenly distributed. Income tax with rising rates is an example.

A regressive tax takes a smaller proportion of income as income rises, so it falls more heavily on people with low incomes. A sales tax on necessities is an example.

Explain 4 marks Explain two reasons for a government to put a tax on cigarettes. (Feb/March 2021, P22)
ReminderTwo reasons, each developed.

A tax raises revenue. Demand for cigarettes is likely to be price inelastic, so many smokers keep buying and the government can collect a large sum.

A tax may discourage smoking. Cigarettes are a demerit good with health and external costs, so a higher price could reduce consumption and harm to others.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse how raising indirect taxes could affect tax revenue and the way income is distributed. (Oct/Nov 2020, P22)
ReminderCover both effects.

Indirect taxes are usually regressive. Poorer households may pay a larger share of income, so income could become less evenly distributed. This may be offset if the extra revenue is spent on benefits for low-income groups.

Revenue is likely to rise, especially where demand is price inelastic, as with basic food or fuel. It could fall if demand is elastic and sales drop sharply, or if informal trading increases.
ig-fiscal-definition:
Explain 4 marks Explain two measures of fiscal policy that could cut poverty. (May/June 2020, P22)
ReminderFiscal policy means government spending and taxation.

The government could raise state benefits. Unemployed people and others on low incomes would have more to spend on basic needs.

It could spend more on education. People may gain skills that help them into better paid jobs, raising their incomes.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse how a government could use fiscal policy to raise employment. (Feb/March 2024, P22)
ReminderUse spending and tax changes and link each to jobs.

Higher government spending or lower taxes may raise total demand. Firms could expand output and take on more workers, reducing cyclical unemployment.

Spending on education and training may raise skills and make workers more employable. Infrastructure spending could attract firms. Lower income tax may increase the incentive to work, and a lower tax on profits could encourage investment and hiring.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not full employment can be reached through fiscal policy. (May/June 2024, P21)
ReminderSeparate cyclical unemployment from frictional and structural.

More government spending or lower taxes raise total demand. Cyclical unemployment may fall as firms hire more. Spending on training and job information could reduce structural and frictional unemployment.

The change may be too small, and households and firms may save any extra income if confidence is low. Exports could fall in a world recession, workers may be immobile, and higher benefits might weaken the incentive to work.

Fiscal policy is likely to reduce unemployment when demand is weak, but full employment may also require supply-side measures that improve mobility and skills.
ig-fiscal-measures:
Explain 4 marks Explain two measures of fiscal policy that could cut poverty. (May/June 2020, P22)
ReminderFiscal policy means government spending and taxation.

The government could raise state benefits. Unemployed people and others on low incomes would have more to spend on basic needs.

It could spend more on education. People may gain skills that help them into better paid jobs, raising their incomes.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse how fiscal policy could give firms a reason to raise output. (May/June 2020, P23)
ReminderLink each tax or spending change to costs, profit or demand.

A cut in the tax on company profits leaves firms with more after tax. They may invest more and expand.

A cut in income tax could raise disposable income and spending, so higher demand may encourage firms to produce more. Subsidies from government spending could lower costs of production, allowing lower prices and more sales.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not fiscal policy works well as a way of cutting poverty. (Oct/Nov 2024, P21)
ReminderGive both sides and judge which measures matter.

Fiscal policy can use benefits, services and taxes. Higher benefits raise the incomes of the poor, and spending on education may lead to better paid jobs. Progressive taxes could fund this help, and lower sales taxes may make necessities cheaper.

However, higher taxes or lower spending elsewhere could cost jobs. More spending may cause inflation, which hurts people on low incomes, and some could rely on benefits and not look for work.

It is likely to cut poverty when help is well targeted and funded fairly. Lasting results may depend on growth and education, which take time.
ig-fiscal-aims:
Analyse 6 marks Analyse how cyclical unemployment could be reduced by cutting taxes and raising government spending. (May/June 2021, P23)
ReminderCyclical unemployment comes from low total demand.

Cyclical unemployment arises when total demand is too low. Lower income tax raises disposable income, so consumption may rise. Lower taxes on profits could encourage investment.

Government spending on projects such as roads adds directly to demand. Firms are likely to see higher sales and profits, increase output and employ more workers.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not cutting government spending will raise unemployment. (Oct/Nov 2023, P23)
ReminderWeigh lost demand against gains from lower taxes or borrowing.

Lower spending reduces total demand. Public sector jobs may be cut and firms that supply the government could lose orders, raising cyclical unemployment. Less spending on training may increase structural unemployment.

However, the cut may allow lower taxes or interest rates, which could raise private spending and investment. Lower benefits might encourage people to take jobs, and demand from households or exports could be rising anyway.

Unemployment is likely to rise if the cut is large and the economy is weak. In a booming economy the private sector may absorb the workers.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not unemployment will fall if a government spends more. (May/June 2020, P21)
ReminderConsider what the money is spent on and the state of the economy.

More spending may raise total demand, so firms could take on more workers. Spending on education and health may make people more employable, and subsidies could help firms expand.

Higher benefits might lead some people to delay taking a job. At full employment extra spending may mainly cause inflation. Training may give the wrong skills, and firms could buy more machines instead of hiring.

A fall is likely where there is spare capacity and the spending is targeted at jobs and skills. Otherwise the effect may be small.
ig-fiscal-policy:
Explain 4 marks Explain how a proportional system of income tax differs from a progressive one. (Oct/Nov 2022, P22)
ReminderSay what happens to the percentage taken as income rises.

Under a proportional system everyone pays the same percentage of income, so the rate does not change as income rises and the distribution of income is largely unaffected.

Under a progressive system the percentage taken rises as income rises, so higher earners pay a larger share, which may narrow the gap between rich and poor.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse how a government could use fiscal policy to raise employment. (Feb/March 2024, P22)
ReminderUse spending and tax changes and link each to jobs.

Higher government spending or lower taxes may raise total demand. Firms could expand output and take on more workers, reducing cyclical unemployment.

Spending on education and training may raise skills and make workers more employable. Infrastructure spending could attract firms. Lower income tax may increase the incentive to work, and a lower tax on profits could encourage investment and hiring.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not full employment can be reached through fiscal policy. (May/June 2024, P21)
ReminderSeparate cyclical unemployment from frictional and structural.

More government spending or lower taxes raise total demand. Cyclical unemployment may fall as firms hire more. Spending on training and job information could reduce structural and frictional unemployment.

The change may be too small, and households and firms may save any extra income if confidence is low. Exports could fall in a world recession, workers may be immobile, and higher benefits might weaken the incentive to work.

Fiscal policy is likely to reduce unemployment when demand is weak, but full employment may also require supply-side measures that improve mobility and skills.
ig-supply-side-definition:
Analyse 6 marks Analyse the ways in which supply-side policies could bring unemployment down. (Oct/Nov 2023, P22)
ReminderChoose policies and show how each leads to more people in work.

Education and training may raise skills and mobility, so more workers could fill vacancies and structural unemployment may fall.

Lower income tax or unemployment benefit may increase the incentive to take a job quickly. Lower taxes on profits and deregulation could encourage firms to invest, expand and hire. Infrastructure spending may cut firms’ costs and help workers travel to jobs.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not supply-side policies, if used, will bring unemployment down. (May/June 2022, P21)
ReminderGive two sides and consider time, cost and demand.

Training may give workers the skills employers want and make them more mobile. Lower income tax or benefits could raise the incentive to work, and subsidies or deregulation may encourage firms to hire.

However, training may be in the wrong areas and takes time. Privatised firms could cut jobs to reduce costs, and lower benefits may not help if there are too few vacancies.

These policies are likely to reduce structural and frictional unemployment. Where total demand is weak, they may have limited effect without demand-side support.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not economic growth is bound to follow from using supply-side policy measures. (May/June 2022, P23)
ReminderTest the word "bound": find cases where growth may not follow.

Education and training may raise productivity. Lower direct taxes could increase incentives to work and invest, and deregulation and privatisation may raise competition and efficiency, so output could grow.

However, the measures may take years and can be costly. Tax cuts may be saved, privatised firms could become private monopolies, and with weak demand firms may not use extra capacity.

They may raise the potential to grow, but growth is not certain. It is likely to depend on the policy chosen, how well it is carried out and the level of total demand.
ig-growth-measurement:
Define 2 marks Define GDP per head. (May/June 2022, P23)
ReminderTotal GDP shared by the population.

GDP per head is a country’s total gross domestic product, the value of its output, divided by its population.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not an economy is worse off for having a lower GDP. (May/June 2021, P23)
ReminderWeigh living standards against environmental and other gains.

Lower GDP is likely to mean lower incomes and less spending. Living standards and employment may be lower, and less tax revenue could limit health care and education.

However, less production may mean less pollution and resource depletion, shorter working hours and lower inflation. Imports could fall, and GDP per head may still be high if the population is small.

It is likely to be a disadvantage in a low-income country with a growing population. Judging it fairly needs GDP per head, its distribution and other measures of welfare.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not living standards are better in high GDP countries than in low GDP ones. (May/June 2024, P21)
ReminderGDP is total output, so consider population and distribution.

High GDP may mean higher incomes, so people could afford better housing, food, health care and education, and life expectancy may be higher.

However, a large population could make GDP per head low. Income may be unevenly shared, prices may be higher, and long hours, pollution and congestion could reduce welfare. A large informal sector may make low GDP understate living standards.

People in high GDP countries may often live better, but GDP per head, its distribution and indicators such as HDI are needed before judging.
ig-unemployment-definitions:
Define 2 marks Define full employment. (Oct/Nov 2022, P22)
ReminderThe lowest level of unemployment likely to be achievable.

Full employment is where unemployment is as low as it is likely to get, so that those willing and able to work can find jobs, although some frictional unemployment may remain.

Define 2 marks Define what is meant by a country’s labour force. (May/June 2021, P21)
ReminderThe economically active: employed and unemployed.

The labour force is made up of people who are willing and able to work, including both the employed and the unemployed.

Explain 4 marks Explain two reasons why a country’s labour force may grow. (May/June 2023, P21)
ReminderTwo causes, each developed.

There may be immigration. Many migrants are of working age, so more people are available for work.

The retirement age may be raised. People would be likely to stay in work for longer.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse reasons for more women joining the labour force of a country. (Feb/March 2022, P22)
ReminderDevelop several linked reasons.

Higher pay and less discrimination may make work more rewarding. Better education for girls could raise their skills and the demand for their labour.

A lower birth rate and more childcare may make it easier to combine work and family. Growth of the tertiary sector, flexible hours and part-time jobs could create suitable openings. A higher cost of living may mean more households need a second income.
ig-absolute-comparative-advantage:
Explain 4 marks A country may change what it specialises in. Explain two reasons for this. (Oct/Nov 2023, P21)
ReminderThink about resources, costs, demand and competition.

Its resources may change, for example through new technology or a mineral discovery. It could then produce a different product at a lower cost.

Demand may change. If consumers buy less of its main product, revenue may fall and resources could move to goods in higher demand.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not consumers gain when countries specialise. (May/June 2021, P21)
ReminderFocus on consumers: price, quality, choice and supply.

Countries may specialise in what they produce best, so output and quality could rise while costs and prices fall. Trade may give consumers more products and better paid jobs.

However, one country could gain monopoly power and raise prices. Reliance on imports may cut off supplies if there is war, bad weather or a trade dispute, and standards of safety may be lower elsewhere.

Consumers are likely to gain where there is competition between several suppliers. Gains may be smaller if a few countries control essential goods.
ig-allocation-questions:
State 2 marks State two of the key questions of resource allocation. (May/June 2020, P22)
ReminderWhat, how and for whom.

What to produce. How to produce it.

Explain 4 marks Explain two of the key decisions about allocating resources. (May/June 2024, P23)
ReminderName each decision and say what it involves.

One decision is what to produce. An economy has to choose, for example, between consumer goods and capital goods.

Another is how to produce. It has to choose methods, such as using more labour or more capital, ideally the most efficient.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse how the three key questions of resource allocation are answered by the price mechanism. (Oct/Nov 2021, P23)
ReminderDemand and supply set prices. Cover what, how and for whom.

The price mechanism means that demand and supply determine prices in a market. What to produce: higher demand raises price and profit, signalling firms to make more.

How to produce: firms are likely to use the cheapest method, for example more machines if wages rise. For whom: goods go to those able to pay, so people whose labour is in demand and who earn more can buy more.
ig-supply-movements:
Analyse 6 marks Analyse what could cause the supply curve of chocolate to shift to the right. (Feb/March 2022, P22)
ReminderA rightward shift comes from a factor other than the price of chocolate.

A shift to the right means more is supplied at each price. Lower costs, such as cheaper wages or transport, could raise profit and supply.

A good cocoa harvest may lower the price of the main raw material. Better technology could raise productivity. A subsidy or lower indirect tax may make chocolate more profitable to make.
ig-market-equilibrium:
Define 2 marks Define disequilibrium in a market. (Oct/Nov 2021, P21)
ReminderQuantity demanded and quantity supplied differ.

Market disequilibrium is where quantity demanded is not equal to quantity supplied, so there is a shortage or a surplus.

Explain 4 marks Explain how price changes can take a market from disequilibrium back to equilibrium. (Oct/Nov 2023, P22)
ReminderCover a shortage or surplus and the price change.

If there is a shortage, with demand above supply, price is likely to rise, reducing quantity demanded and raising quantity supplied until they are equal.

If there is a surplus, with supply above demand, price is likely to fall, raising quantity demanded and reducing quantity supplied until the market clears.
ig-ped-determinants:
Identify 2 marks Identify two things that determine price elasticity of demand. (Oct/Nov 2022, P23)
ReminderSubstitutes, share of income, necessity, habit, time.

The availability of substitutes. The proportion of income spent on the product.

Explain 4 marks Explain why the price elasticity of demand for soap is likely to be lower than for a luxury brand of perfume. (May/June 2022, P22)
ReminderCompare the two products on two factors.

Soap is a necessity while luxury perfume is a want, so people are likely to keep buying soap when its price rises but may give up the perfume.

Soap usually takes a small share of income, so a price rise is hardly noticed, whereas dearer perfume could be put off.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse why the price elasticity of demand for salt is likely to differ from that for one brand of luxury chocolates. (Feb/March 2024, P22)
ReminderApply determinants to both products.

One brand of chocolates has many substitutes and is a want. A higher price may lead buyers to switch, so demand is likely to be price elastic.

It may also take a larger share of income and can be put off. Salt has few substitutes, is seen as a necessity and costs little, so quantity demanded is likely to change by a smaller percentage than price.
ig-ped-significance:
Analyse 6 marks Analyse how a firm may gain from selling a product with price-inelastic demand. (May/June 2021, P23)
ReminderLink inelastic demand to price, revenue and profit.

With inelastic demand, quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price. A rise in price is therefore likely to raise total revenue.

Profit may increase if costs do not rise as much, for example for a firm selling an essential medicine. Sales may also be more stable, making planning easier, and inelastic demand could reflect little competition.

Analyse 6 marks The price of milk rises. Analyse the possible effects on the revenue of milk producers and of soft drinks producers. (May/June 2023, P22)
ReminderUse PED for milk and substitution for soft drinks.

A higher price is likely to reduce the quantity of milk demanded. If demand is inelastic, quantity falls by a smaller percentage, so milk producers’ revenue may rise. If demand is elastic, their revenue could fall.

Soft drinks may be substitutes for milk. Some buyers could switch, raising demand for soft drinks and the revenue of their producers.
ig-pes-determinants:
Define 2 marks Define inelastic supply. (Oct/Nov 2022, P22)
ReminderCompare the two percentage changes.

Inelastic supply is where quantity supplied changes by a smaller percentage than price, giving a price elasticity of supply below 1.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse what affects whether the supply of a product is elastic or inelastic. (Feb/March 2025, P22)
ReminderStocks, capacity, time, production period, mobility.

Price elasticity of supply measures how responsive quantity supplied is to price. If a product can be stored, firms may release stocks quickly, making supply elastic.

Spare capacity could let output rise easily. A long production period, as for crops, is likely to make supply inelastic. Over a longer time, and with mobile resources, supply may become more elastic.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse the main influences on a product’s price elasticity of supply. (Oct/Nov 2023, P21)
ReminderDevelop two or more determinants with a chain each.

Stocks matter. With plenty of unsold goods, a firm could raise supply quickly, so supply may be elastic.

Spare capacity, such as idle workers, has a similar effect. In the short run at least one factor is fixed, so supply is likely to be inelastic, while in the long run it may be elastic. Goods that are quick and simple to make, such as bread, may have more elastic supply than smartphones.
ig-market-system:
Explain 4 marks Explain two ways consumers may benefit from a market economic system. (Oct/Nov 2020, P23)
ReminderTwo benefits, each developed.

Consumers may have sovereignty. Their spending signals what firms should produce, so output is likely to match their wants.

Competition between firms may be strong. Firms could keep prices low and quality high to hold on to customers.

Explain 4 marks Explain why a market economic system would not provide public goods. (Oct/Nov 2022, P22)
ReminderNon-excludable and non-rival.

Public goods are non-excludable. People who do not pay can still use them, so there are likely to be free riders.

Private firms aim for profit. If they cannot charge users, they are unlikely to earn revenue and so would not supply the goods.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not an economy gains from having a market economic system. (May/June 2022, P21)
ReminderBenefits of competition against market failure.

Competition and the profit motive may raise efficiency. Prices could be low, quality and choice high, resources may move to what consumers want, and growth could be strong.

However, markets may fail. Public goods may not be supplied, merit goods under-consumed and demerit goods over-consumed. Pollution, unemployment and unequal incomes could result.

A market system is likely to benefit an economy where competition is strong. Some government action may still be needed to deal with market failure and protect the poor.
ig-market-system-evaluation:
Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not a market economy gives the best possible allocation of resources. (May/June 2023, P22)
ReminderPrice signals against market failure.

Prices change with demand and supply, so resources may move from goods that are less wanted to goods that are more wanted. Profit and competition could keep costs and prices down.

However, merit goods may be under-consumed and demerit goods over-consumed. Public goods may not be made, external costs ignored, monopolies could restrict output and resources may be immobile.

It may allocate many private goods well, but is unlikely to give the best allocation where market failure is serious. Government action could help, though it can also fail.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not a market economy is likely to have a lot of poverty. (Oct/Nov 2024, P22)
ReminderSeparate absolute from relative poverty.

With no or few welfare benefits, those who cannot work may have little income. Unemployment and unequal pay could leave some poor, merit goods such as education may be under-consumed, and monopolies may charge high prices.

Competition and the profit motive may encourage efficiency and low prices. Faster growth could raise incomes and create jobs, so absolute poverty may be low even if relative poverty remains.

Poverty is likely to be high where many people lack skills or cannot work. A productive economy with plenty of jobs may have much less, although inequality could persist.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not the disadvantages of a market economic system can be overcome by government intervention. (Oct/Nov 2024, P23)
ReminderMatch each market failure to a policy, then consider government failure.

A government can provide public goods and subsidise merit goods. Taxes or regulation may limit demerit goods and pollution, monopolies can be controlled, and benefits or a minimum wage may help people on low incomes.

However, the government may lack accurate information. Taxes may be set at the wrong level, policies can be costly, and rules may weaken incentives or create shortages, causing government failure.

Intervention is likely to reduce many disadvantages but may not remove them. Success depends on good information, enforcement and the size of the costs.
ig-market-failure-causes:
Define 2 marks Define market failure. (May/June 2020, P23)
ReminderThe market does not allocate resources efficiently.

Market failure happens when the market forces of demand and supply do not lead to an efficient allocation of resources.

Explain 4 marks Using an example of each, explain what separates a merit good from a public good. (May/June 2023, P21)
ReminderUnder-consumed against not provided at all.

A merit good, such as education, is more beneficial than consumers realise, so it is likely to be under-consumed in a free market.

A public good, such as street lighting, is non-excludable and non-rival, so private firms are unlikely to supply it and the government may need to pay for it.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse why markets can fail. (May/June 2022, P23)
ReminderDevelop several causes rather than listing them.

Market failure is an inefficient allocation of resources. Consumers may lack information, so merit goods are under-consumed and demerit goods over-consumed.

Producers and consumers may ignore external costs, leading to over-production of goods that pollute. Public goods may not be supplied because of free riders. A monopoly could restrict output and raise price, and immobile workers may stay unemployed.
ig-mixed-system:
Define 2 marks Define a mixed economic system. (Feb/March 2021, P22)
ReminderBoth sectors play a part.

A mixed economic system has both a public sector, run by the government, and a private sector in which market forces operate.

Explain 4 marks Explain what separates the private sector from the public sector. (Oct/Nov 2024, P23)
ReminderCompare ownership and aims.

The private sector is owned and run by individuals and firms, whose decisions are usually guided by self-interest, such as profit.

The public sector is owned and run by the government, whose decisions are usually guided by the welfare of society.

Explain 4 marks In a mixed economic system, explain the way the main decisions on allocating resources get made. (Feb/March 2025, P22)
ReminderCover both the market and the government.

In the private sector, firms and consumers decide through the price mechanism, with demand, supply and the profit motive guiding what is made and how.

In the public sector, the government decides, using spending, taxes and regulation to pursue the welfare of society.
ig-money:
Identify 2 marks Identify two jobs that money does. (May/June 2023, P21)
ReminderThe four functions.

It acts as a medium of exchange. It acts as a store of value.

Explain 4 marks Money has certain characteristics. Explain two of them. (May/June 2024, P22)
ReminderName each and say why it matters.

Money needs to be generally acceptable, so people are willing to take it in payment or to settle a debt.

It needs to be divisible, so it can be split into smaller units to pay for items of different prices.

Explain 4 marks Explain two benefits of using banknotes as money. (May/June 2020, P22)
ReminderLink each benefit to everyday use.

Banknotes are portable. They are light, so people can carry them easily to make payments.

They are recognisable. Their distinct features help people know they are genuine currency, so they are likely to be accepted.
ig-banking:
Define 2 marks Define a central bank. (Oct/Nov 2024, P23)
ReminderOwnership and main roles.

A central bank is usually a government-owned bank that carries out monetary policy and provides banking services to the government and commercial banks.

Explain 4 marks Explain two things that a central bank does. (Oct/Nov 2023, P23)
ReminderTwo functions, each developed.

It operates monetary policy. For example, it may set the interest rate to help control inflation.

It acts as lender of last resort. It may lend to commercial banks that are short of money, helping to keep the banking system stable.

Explain 4 marks Explain two services that commercial banks can provide for firms. (May/June 2023, P23)
ReminderLink each to a business need.

Banks provide loans and overdrafts. Firms could use them to pay for expansion or day to day costs.

Banks help to process payments. Online transfers let firms pay suppliers and receive money from customers quickly.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not economic growth will rise if commercial banks lend more. (Oct/Nov 2022, P23)
ReminderConsider who borrows, what for and spare capacity.

Households may borrow to spend more and firms to invest. Higher total demand could raise output and employment, and investment may increase productive capacity.

However, loans may be spent on imports or used to pay old debts. At full employment more demand may cause inflation rather than growth, and later repayments or higher interest could cut spending.

Growth is more likely if the loans finance investment and there is spare capacity. Lending mainly for consumption could give only a short rise.
ig-households:
Explain 4 marks A household with a high income may borrow more than one with a low income. Explain two reasons. (Feb/March 2022, P22)
ReminderThink about lenders and borrowers.

Banks may be more willing to lend to it, because they are more confident of being repaid.

It may own more assets, which could be offered as security for a large loan, for example to buy an expensive house.

Explain 4 marks Explain how spending and borrowing are each affected when confidence is low. (Oct/Nov 2022, P21)
ReminderCover both.

Low confidence is likely to reduce spending, as households may save in case they lose their jobs.

It is also likely to reduce borrowing, as people may fear they will be unable to repay.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse reasons for households borrowing more in one country than in another. (Feb/March 2021, P22)
ReminderCompare interest rates, confidence, banks and culture.

The interest rate may be lower in one country, making borrowing cheaper.

Households may be more confident of repaying if jobs and incomes are growing. Banks may have more funds and lend more easily. Debt may be more socially acceptable, or the population younger. Low incomes could also force people to borrow for necessities.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not governments ought to encourage people to save more. (Feb/March 2022, P22)
ReminderWeigh future security and investment against lower demand.

More saving may provide funds for investment and a safety net for households. Lower spending could reduce demand-pull inflation and imports, and people may be better prepared for retirement.

However, less spending lowers total demand, so growth may slow and cyclical unemployment rise. Indirect tax revenue may fall, and some people are too poor to save.

Encouraging saving is likely to be sensible when inflation is high or saving is very low. In a recession it could make matters worse.
ig-occupation-choice:
Explain 4 marks Explain two reasons why a person might choose a career as a doctor. (Feb/March 2023, P22)
ReminderUse one wage and one non-wage reason.

Doctors are likely to be well paid, so the person could enjoy a high standard of living.

They may want to help people, so the work could give high job satisfaction.

Explain 4 marks Explain two reasons why people who work in building may not move into teaching. (Feb/March 2025, P22)
ReminderThink about mobility and rewards.

They may lack the qualifications needed, so they would be occupationally immobile without further training.

Building may pay more, so changing job could lower their standard of living.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse reasons why someone who acts for a living might switch to teaching. (Feb/March 2021, P22)
ReminderInclude wage and non-wage factors.

Teaching may offer a higher or steadier income, allowing a better standard of living.

Job security is likely to be greater, as actors often have gaps between jobs. Hours and holidays may suit family life. Conditions and pensions may be better, and helping children learn could give satisfaction.
ig-wage-determination:
Analyse 6 marks Analyse what might cause the pay of bank workers to rise. (Oct/Nov 2020, P22)
ReminderUse demand, supply and bargaining power.

Demand for bank workers may rise if more people use banks or workers become more productive. Banks would compete for them, pushing wages up.

Supply may fall if higher qualifications are required. A trade union could bargain for more pay, higher bank profits may fund bonuses, and inflation may lead workers to seek rises.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse reasons why pay for teachers as a whole might rise. (Oct/Nov 2022, P22)
ReminderDemand, supply, unions and government.

Demand may rise if there are more pupils or classes are made smaller. Schools would compete for teachers, raising wages.

Supply may fall if training takes longer or other jobs pay more. Stronger unions could bargain for higher pay, and a government that favours education may agree to raise it.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not poverty will be cut by a national minimum wage. (May/June 2020, P21)
ReminderA diagram can help. Say who is covered.

A minimum wage set above equilibrium raises the pay of low earners, so they could afford more necessities and the gap with higher earners may narrow. Better motivation and more spending might even support jobs.

However, firms’ costs rise and they may employ fewer workers. It does not help people who cannot work, may be set too low to matter, and higher paid workers could demand rises to keep their differential.

It is likely to cut poverty if set at a moderate level and enforced. Other help may be needed for those out of work.
ig-wage-differences:
Explain 4 marks Explain two reasons why pay may be higher in the tertiary sector than in the primary sector. (Oct/Nov 2020, P23)
ReminderUse demand and supply.

Demand for tertiary workers may be higher, as service industries are expanding and workers may be more productive.

Their supply may be lower, because many jobs require qualifications and long training.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse possible reasons for women being paid less than men. (May/June 2024, P21)
ReminderDevelop causes rather than asserting them.

Some employers may discriminate and undervalue women’s work, especially where laws are weak. Their pay could then be held down.

Women may have had less education or taken breaks to raise children, so have less experience and fewer promoted posts. They may be concentrated in low-paid or part-time jobs and have weaker bargaining power.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not a skilled worker is always paid more than an unskilled one. (Feb/March 2020, P22)
ReminderTest the word "always" with exceptions.

Skilled workers may be scarce because training takes time. Their productivity and demand may be high, supply inelastic and bargaining power strong, so wages are likely to be higher.

However, a skill in a declining industry may be in low demand. Unskilled workers could earn more for dangerous or unpleasant work, long hours or strong union membership, and a new skilled worker may earn little.

Skilled workers usually earn more, but not always. It depends on demand and supply in each labour market and on bargaining power.
ig-labour-mobility:
Define 2 marks Define labour mobility. (Oct/Nov 2024, P21)
ReminderOccupational and geographical.

Labour mobility is the ability of workers to move to another job, either by changing occupation or by changing where they work.

Explain 4 marks Explain two factors affecting how mobile labour is. (Oct/Nov 2022, P21)
ReminderName each and show its effect.

Training opportunities matter. Where retraining is easy to get, workers could switch occupation more readily.

The cost of housing matters. Where homes are affordable, workers may find it easier to move for a job.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse what influences how easily workers can move between jobs. (May/June 2020, P22)
ReminderOccupational and geographical mobility.

Occupational mobility depends on education and training. Workers with more skills are likely to have a wider choice of jobs.

Geographical mobility depends on the price and availability of housing. Family ties, such as children in school, may stop people moving. Immigration controls could limit movement between countries.
ig-division-of-labour:
Define 2 marks Define the division of labour. (Oct/Nov 2021, P23)
ReminderProduction split into tasks.

Division of labour is where production is broken into separate tasks and each worker specialises in one of them.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse the ways a firm may gain from dividing up labour. (Oct/Nov 2020, P23)
ReminderLink specialisation to output, cost and profit.

Workers who specialise in one task may become quicker and better at it. Productivity and quality could rise.

Training may be shorter and less equipment needed, lowering costs. Lower prices or better products could raise demand, revenue and profit.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not the division of labour is good for workers. (May/June 2020, P23)
ReminderBenefits and costs to workers, not firms.

Specialising may raise workers’ skill and productivity, so they could earn higher pay. Training may be short, and people can do the job they are best at.

However, repeating one task can be boring. Narrow skills may make it hard to change job, so unemployment could follow if demand falls or machines take over the task.

Workers are likely to benefit where specialisation brings skill and higher pay. Those doing simple repetitive tasks may gain less.
ig-types-of-firms:
Identify 2 marks Identify two primary sector industries besides farming. (May/June 2021, P21)
ReminderIndustries that extract or collect natural resources.

Mining. Fishing.

Explain 4 marks Explain two difficulties that small firms face. (May/June 2020, P21)
ReminderTwo challenges, each developed.

Small firms may find it hard to raise finance, as banks may see them as risky, which could limit expansion.

They may lack economies of scale, so their average costs could be higher than those of large rivals, making it harder to compete on price.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse why small firms continue to exist. (Oct/Nov 2022, P21)
ReminderMarket size, barriers, owners’ aims and costs.

Barriers to entry may be low, so people can start firms with little capital.

Some serve a niche or local market that is too small for large firms. Owners may want to keep control, governments may give support, and some find it hard to borrow. Where economies of scale are small, a small firm may have low enough costs to survive.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not a small firm is more likely than a large one to go out of business. (May/June 2023, P22)
ReminderCompare finance, costs, loyalty and flexibility.

Small firms may have higher average costs without economies of scale. They could find loans harder to get, have little retained profit and be new with inexperienced owners.

However, they may be flexible, give personal service and serve a loyal niche market. They may get government help, while large firms could suffer diseconomies of scale.

Small firms are often more at risk, especially in a recession. A well run small firm with loyal customers may outlast a badly run large one.
ig-mergers:
Explain 4 marks Describe two kinds of merger, explaining each. (Oct/Nov 2022, P21)
ReminderName the type and say which firms join.

A horizontal merger joins firms at the same stage of production in the same industry, such as two supermarkets.

A vertical merger joins firms in one industry but at separate stages of making the product, such as a car maker and a tyre maker.

Explain 4 marks Explain two ways a firm may benefit from a horizontal merger. (Oct/Nov 2022, P23)
ReminderMarket share and economies of scale are the usual routes.

The firm is likely to gain market share, and with fewer competitors it may be able to raise prices.

It may gain economies of scale, such as bulk buying, which could lower average costs and raise profit.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse why a government might stop a horizontal merger from going ahead. (May/June 2024, P21)
ReminderFocus on harm to consumers, jobs and the economy.

A horizontal merger joins firms at the same stage in the same industry. The new firm could gain monopoly power, causing market failure.

With less competition, prices may rise and quality, choice and innovation fall. Jobs may be cut, and diseconomies of scale could make the firm less competitive abroad.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not firms should be encouraged by their government to merge. (May/June 2023, P21)
ReminderEconomies of scale against market power.

Merged firms may gain economies of scale, so costs and prices could fall, quality improve and exports rise. Higher profits may raise tax revenue.

However, the merger may create a monopoly with higher prices and less choice. Diseconomies of scale could raise costs and some workers may lose their jobs.

Encouragement is likely to make sense where firms are small and face large foreign rivals. Where it would greatly reduce competition at home, the government should be cautious.
ig-economies-of-scale:
Define 2 marks Define diseconomies of scale. (Feb/March 2022, P22)
ReminderAverage cost and scale.

Diseconomies of scale are rises in average cost of production that happen when a firm or industry grows too large.

Identify 2 marks Identify two kinds of internal economies of scale. (May/June 2022, P23)
ReminderPurchasing, technical, financial, managerial, marketing, risk-bearing.

Purchasing economies. Technical economies.

Explain 4 marks Explain two benefits of being a large firm. (Oct/Nov 2023, P21)
ReminderTwo advantages, each developed.

A large firm may gain purchasing economies, buying in bulk at a discount, which lowers average cost.

It may find it easier to borrow, possibly at lower interest, so it can invest and grow.

Analyse 6 marks A school grows in size. Analyse the economies of scale it could benefit from. (Feb/March 2024, P22)
ReminderApply each type to a school.

Economies of scale lower average cost, here the cost per student. Purchasing economies: desks or computers could be bought in bulk at a discount.

It may employ specialist teachers and an accountant. It could afford equipment such as a media studio and use it fully, and may borrow more cheaply.
ig-factor-demand:
Explain 4 marks Explain two things that influence how much of a factor of production firms demand. (May/June 2024, P22)
ReminderThink about product demand and factor prices.

Demand for the product matters. If it rises, firms are likely to want more factors to produce more, so factor demand is derived.

The price of the factor matters. If wages rise, a firm may demand less labour and use more capital.

Explain 4 marks A firm spends on the newest technology. Explain two things it may give up as a result. (May/June 2023, P23)
ReminderOpportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone.

It may give up higher wages, so it could struggle to keep skilled workers.

It may give up advertising, losing the chance to raise demand for its product.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse the factors that influence how many workers a farmer wants to employ. (Oct/Nov 2023, P22)
ReminderDemand for output, wages, productivity and capital.

Labour demand is derived from demand for the food produced. Higher food demand may lead the farmer to expand and hire.

Lower wages make workers cheaper, and more skilled workers are more productive. Cheaper machinery could replace workers. Farm size, subsidies and the season, such as harvest, also matter.
ig-labour-capital-intensive:
Explain 4 marks Explain how a labour-intensive industry differs from a capital-intensive one. (Oct/Nov 2021, P21)
ReminderCompare the factor used most, with examples.

A labour-intensive industry uses a high proportion of workers compared with capital, for example hairdressing.

A capital-intensive industry relies mainly on machinery and equipment, for example oil refining.

Explain 4 marks A firm chooses labour-intensive production. Explain two possible reasons. (Oct/Nov 2024, P22)
ReminderCost, productivity or the type of product.

Wages may be low, so labour could be cheaper than capital and keep costs down.

The firm may sell personal services, where customers expect individual attention that machines are unlikely to give.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse reasons for a firm moving towards more capital-intensive production. (May/June 2021, P22)
ReminderCosts, technology, reliability and labour supply.

Capital may become cheaper or wages may rise. Using machines could then lower costs and raise profit.

Better technology may raise productivity and quality. Machines can run for long hours without strikes or sickness. A labour shortage, lower interest rates or subsidies on equipment may also encourage the change.
ig-production-productivity:
Identify 2 marks Identify two things that could cause labour productivity to rise. (Feb/March 2023, P22)
ReminderOutput per worker.

Better training. Better quality capital equipment.

Explain 4 marks Explain two methods a firm could use to make its workers more productive. (May/June 2021, P21)
ReminderMethod and effect on output per worker.

The firm could provide training, which may raise workers’ skills so each produces more.

It could introduce performance-related pay, which may motivate workers to work harder.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse reasons for productivity being low in a country. (May/June 2020, P22)
ReminderSkills, capital, health and motivation.

Education and training may be poor, so workers lack skills and produce less per hour.

Low investment may leave them using old equipment. Poor health care could mean tired or absent workers, and low pay and bad conditions may reduce motivation.
ig-costs-definitions:
Define 2 marks Define a fixed cost, giving an example. (Oct/Nov 2023, P22)
ReminderDefinition plus example.

A fixed cost is one that does not change when output changes, even when output is zero, for example the rent of a factory.

Analyse 6 marks With the help of a diagram, analyse what happens to total fixed cost (TFC) and average fixed cost (AFC) as output rises. (Feb/March 2022, P22)
ReminderDraw cost on the vertical axis and output on the horizontal axis: TFC is flat and AFC slopes down.

Total fixed cost does not change as output rises in the short run, so on the diagram it is a horizontal line starting on the cost axis.

Average fixed cost is TFC divided by output. The same total is spread over more units, so AFC falls and its curve slopes downwards. It gets closer to the output axis but does not reach zero.
ig-costs-calculation:
Define 2 marks Define a fixed cost, giving an example. (Oct/Nov 2023, P22)
ReminderDefinition plus example.

A fixed cost is one that does not change when output changes, even when output is zero, for example the rent of a factory.

Analyse 6 marks With the help of a diagram, analyse what happens to total fixed cost (TFC) and average fixed cost (AFC) as output rises. (Feb/March 2022, P22)
ReminderDraw cost on the vertical axis and output on the horizontal axis: TFC is flat and AFC slopes down.

Total fixed cost does not change as output rises in the short run, so on the diagram it is a horizontal line starting on the cost axis.

Average fixed cost is TFC divided by output. The same total is spread over more units, so AFC falls and its curve slopes downwards. It gets closer to the output axis but does not reach zero.
ig-revenue-definitions:
Define 2 marks Define total revenue. (Oct/Nov 2021, P21)
ReminderPrice times quantity.

Total revenue is all the money a firm receives from selling its products, calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold.

State 2 marks State the way average revenue is worked out. (Oct/Nov 2023, P21)
ReminderRevenue per unit.

Average revenue is total revenue divided by the quantity sold.

Explain 4 marks Explain two reasons for a rise in a firm’s revenue. (May/June 2024, P23)
ReminderDemand and price.

Demand may increase, for example after successful advertising, so the firm sells more and earns more.

The firm may raise its price when demand is inelastic, so quantity falls by a smaller percentage and revenue rises.
ig-revenue-calculation:
Define 2 marks Define total revenue. (Oct/Nov 2021, P21)
ReminderPrice times quantity.

Total revenue is all the money a firm receives from selling its products, calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold.

State 2 marks State the way average revenue is worked out. (Oct/Nov 2023, P21)
ReminderRevenue per unit.

Average revenue is total revenue divided by the quantity sold.

Analyse 6 marks The price of milk rises. Analyse the possible effects on the revenue of milk producers and of soft drinks producers. (May/June 2023, P22)
ReminderUse PED for milk and substitution for soft drinks.

A higher price is likely to reduce the quantity of milk demanded. If demand is inelastic, quantity falls by a smaller percentage, so milk producers’ revenue may rise. If demand is elastic, their revenue could fall.

Soft drinks may be substitutes for milk. Some buyers could switch, raising demand for soft drinks and the revenue of their producers.
ig-firm-objectives:
State 2 marks State two aims a firm may have. (May/June 2020, P21)
ReminderSurvival, profit, growth, social welfare.

Survival. Profit maximisation.

Define 2 marks Define profit maximisation. (May/June 2020, P23)
ReminderThe biggest gap between revenue and cost.

Profit maximisation is producing the level of output at which total revenue exceeds total cost by the largest amount.

Identify 2 marks Identify two social welfare aims that a firm might have. (Oct/Nov 2022, P21)
ReminderAims that help society.

Protecting the environment. Providing jobs for disadvantaged groups.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not growth ought to be the chief objective of a firm. (May/June 2021, P21)
ReminderCompare growth with survival, profit and welfare.

Growth may bring economies of scale and lower average costs, greater market share and more power, and make the firm harder to take over.

However, a new or struggling firm may need to put survival first. A niche market may limit growth, large size could bring diseconomies of scale, profit may fund later growth, and a state firm may aim at social welfare.

Growth is likely to suit a firm in an expanding market with finance available. In a recession or a small market another objective is probably wiser.
ig-competitive-markets:
Analyse 6 marks Analyse what may happen when firms face more competition. (Oct/Nov 2024, P21)
ReminderEffects on consumers and on firms.

Firms may cut prices to attract buyers, which benefits consumers but could force weak firms to close.

They may improve quality, innovate and offer more choice. Spending on advertising could raise costs, while sharing customers among more firms is likely to reduce each firm’s profit.

Analyse 6 marks Analyse how consumers may gain when a market is competitive. (Oct/Nov 2024, P22)
ReminderPrice, quality, choice and responsiveness.

A competitive market has many firms and few barriers to entry, giving substitutes. Firms are likely to keep prices low to win customers.

They may raise quality and innovate. Choice could be wide, and firms may respond quickly to changes in what consumers want.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not a firm is harmed by competition. (May/June 2023, P23)
ReminderLost sales against the spur to improve.

Competition may reduce a firm’s market share, revenue and profit. It may have to cut prices or spend more, leaving less to reinvest.

However, competition could push it to be efficient and innovative. Better, cheaper products may win customers and make it competitive abroad.

Weak or high-cost firms are likely to be harmed. A firm that responds by improving could end up stronger.
ig-monopoly-markets:
Explain 4 marks Explain two features of a monopoly. (Oct/Nov 2024, P23)
ReminderShare of market, barriers, price.

A monopoly is the only firm, or has a dominant share of the market, so consumers have few or no substitutes.

Barriers to entry are high, so new firms find it difficult to join the industry and profits may last.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not buyers gain when one firm becomes a monopoly. (Feb/March 2022, P22)
ReminderEconomies of scale against market power.

A monopoly may have economies of scale, so prices could be lower, and large profits might fund research and better products. A state monopoly may aim to benefit society.

However, it may raise prices and restrict supply. Choice falls, there is less pressure to improve quality, and it could suffer diseconomies of scale.

Consumers may gain if cost savings are passed on or the firm is regulated. Without such pressure they are likely to lose.

Discuss 8 marks Discuss whether or not monopolies ought to be allowed by a government. (Oct/Nov 2020, P23)
ReminderGive both sides and consider regulation.

Monopolies may gain economies of scale and charge low prices. Profits could pay for investment and research, and a large firm may compete abroad. A state monopoly could pursue welfare.

However, they may abuse market power with high prices, low quality and little choice. Resources could be allocated inefficiently and new firms kept out.

They may be allowed where one large firm is far more efficient, provided it is regulated. Otherwise promoting competition is likely to be better.
